newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS - EU leaves door ajar to wheat exports.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - EU leaves door ajar to wheat exports.

text.p: The European Union ended the bulk of its annual wheat export campaign on Thursday, pulling down the shutters on its weekly tender system but leaving the door ajar to exporters seeking last-minute supplies.

Grain officials said the EU Commission closed its tenders for export licences for 1996/97 wheat from the open market, having boosted exports sharply from the previous year, when low stocks and high prices had forced it to introduce an export tax.
But Thursday's decision coincided with fresh awards that added at least 400,000 tonnes to the volume released for export and brought the year's total above 9.6 million tonnes.
"We have done enough," a European grain official said after an EU committee endorsed the Commission's decision to close the weekly export system until sales begin for the next harvest.

Officials are worried about potential damage from dry weather on the next French crop and a recent freeze on part of the U.S. harvest, and have yet to set a date for opening the new July/June export campaign.
The European official said the Commission had earlier on Thursday accepted bids for 217,000 tonnes of soft wheat exports submitted through an alternative daily channel on Tuesday.
These exports are neither subsidised nor taxed but come with short validity so-called nil value licences that carry greater risk since they cannot be prefixed.
That move followed EU acceptance on Wednesday of 190,000 tonnes at a fixed subsidy of zero, meaning the wheat can be guaranteed to be sold onto the world market at domestic cost.
Further daily bids may be in the pipeline for EU approval under a three-day veto system and the nil value daily licence regime remains open, officials said.
Traders were also waiting for word on bids submitted earlier this week for 400,000 tonnes of flour that could push this week's final export dash still higher.

Those bids were seen as more politically sensitive since they were for export subsidies of five Ecus per tonne, whereas the U.S. has been pushing Brussels to stop assisting flour sales in the face of opposition from its own millers.
Traders said grain exporters were wrapping up the export season as it had begun, toying with the idea of export taxes for licences traded among themselves.

Some shippers were said to be still short of export licences for cargoes of 1996/97 wheat. Apart from the unpredictable daily system, buying previously issued licences from other exporters at a level that implied taxes might be the only sure solution.
Traders said licences issued with subsidies were offered in the secondary market at tax levels on Wednesday and Thursday.
The EU also on Thursday knocked down speculation that the four to five month validity period for licences now in the market (excluding nil value ones) might be reduced to June 30.

Several traders were pondering whether such licences could be kept for new crop wheat in July and August. EU rules would normally prevent this by cutting the subsidised face value of the licence for specified months. But several traders and officials have said current regulations do not allow a licence that is already worth zero to drop into negative figures.
